rationale: The clinical review discusses signs, diagnosis and multidisciplinary care for functional movement disorders. Tremor, pain and fatigue are among its phenotypes. Functional tremor is a distinct diagnostic question. The publication reports neither raw fig and Parkinson rest tremor nor dried date fruit and Parkinson pain comparisons.

The review separates nuclear and cytoplasmic adenosine kinase roles and discusses molecular and neurological research. The original does not compare dried date fruit with Parkinson pain severity.

The Finnish registry study assesses whether responders and nonresponders differ after anterior cervical spine surgery. Postoperative patient-reported outcomes are not a dried date fruit comparison for Parkinson pain.
The original compares spine reconstruction outcomes including radiographic kyphosis in ankylosing spondylitis. The operative comparison does not assign dried dates or measure Parkinson pain severity.
The review distinguishes acute pain after fracture from pain that persists after healing and discusses assessment. It supplies no dried date fruit or Parkinson pain intervention.
The experimental study concerns gentiopicroside and motor or cellular measurements in a mouse model. The isolated compound is not raw fig and its model findings do not test clinical rest tremor.

The Parkinson interview study uses videos of falls to study empathy for pain and qualitatively describes two patterns of experience. Viewing simulated events provides no recurrent-fall estimate by raw orange intake.
The randomized pilot tests a return-to-work program after cancer and reports recruitment, retention and adherence. Neither arm tests dried date fruit or provides a Parkinson pain contrast.

The synthesis compares injection treatments for painful post-stroke limb spasticity at different times after stroke. Its drug and post-stroke comparisons do not measure dried-date effects on Parkinson pain.

The clinical review describes acute febrile syndromes with rigidity and their differential diagnosis. This acute emergency literature gives no study of fresh or ground culinary sage for dystonia, rigidity or falls.

The longitudinal ultrasound study compares vagus and sural nerve measurements in fibromyalgia and control participants. Differences in nerve size are unrelated to a dried date fruit intervention for Parkinson pain.

This real-world advanced Parkinson cohort of 802 describes motor and nonmotor symptoms during good ON time. The analysis linked additional good ON time to fewer falls (IRR 0.91, 95% CI 0.87–0.95). The comparison centers on hours of symptom control. It gives no dietary estimates for sage, date fruit or fig across falls, pain, rigidity, rest tremor, apathy or fatigue.
